verdict.rationale: Across four sections of the canon the same word-level pattern keeps appearing: a written, God-originated deposit is the standard, and competing voices are judged against it. Isaiah 8:20 pairs the Hebrew word for written instruction (torah, H8451, queried 204 occurrences, spread across the whole Bible) with the word for testimony (teudah, H8584, only 3 occurrences in the whole Bible) and pronounces the formula of judgment 'no dawn' (ein shachar) on speech that does not match the prior word. Mark 7:8 to 13 sets the commandment (entole) and word (logos) of God (theos) against the tradition (paradosis) of men (anthropoi), using two forensic verbs: 'to set aside, nullify' (atheteo, G0114) and 'to render legally void' (akyroo, G0208). The latter occurs only at Matthew 15:6, Mark 7:13, and Galatians 3:17, and in every case it describes voiding a prior authoritative text. Acts 17:11 has the Bereans 'judicially examine' (anakrino, G0350, a courtroom verb that clusters in legal contexts in Luke, Acts, and 1 Corinthians) the writings (graphai) to test apostolic preaching (logos). 2 Timothy 3:16 to 17 grounds it all: every Scripture (pasa graphe) is 'God-breathed' (theopneustos, G2315, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, that is, a hapax) and sufficient toward (pros) four functions, so that the man of God is 'complete' (artios, G0739, also a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) and fully equipped. The pattern is dense, grammatically overt, and spans Torah, Prophets, Gospels, Acts, and Pastoral Epistles, so the verdict is high-confidence.

scripture.force: The paired construction 'to the instruction and to the testimony' (le-torah ve-li-teudah) names a prior written-revelation standard against which speakers are tested. The 'if-then' clause (the conditional) 'if they do not speak according to this word' (im lo yomeru ka-davar ha-zeh) is followed by the verdict 'there is no dawn for him' (ein lo shachar), with 'there is not' (ayin, H0369) functioning as the standard Hebrew judgment-of-absence formula. 'Instruction' (torah) is well attested (queried 204 occurrences, spread across the whole Bible, covering Law, Prophets, and Writings), so its sense as authoritative instruction is triangulated and stable. 'Testimony' (teudah) occurs only 3 times, and one of those (Ruth 4:7) carries a distinct sense (a legal custom or attestation of a transaction), so the Isaiah sense rests almost entirely on Isaiah 8:16 and 8:20 themselves. The anti-mediumistic frame (Isaiah 8:19) sharpens the force: the prior written deposit outranks competing oracular voices.

Direct antithesis: 'forsaking the commandment of God you hold the tradition of men' (aphentes ten entolen tou theou krateite ten paradosin ton anthropon). The contrast is carried by the two genitives 'of God' (theou) and 'of men' (anthropon), which encode the authority asymmetry at the word level: the divine commandment is the standard, the human tradition is the displacing rival. The decisive word is 'tradition' (paradosis, G3862), which occurs 13 times and is morally neutral in itself: it labels the commended apostolic deposit in 1 Corinthians 11:2 and 2 Thessalonians 2:15 but the condemned human accretion here and in Colossians 2:8 and Galatians 1:14. The origin of the tradition, divine or human, is what the genitive (the 'of-X' grammatical form) specifies, and that is what determines authority.

'You set aside the commandment of God so that you may keep your tradition' (atheteite ten entolen tou theou hina ten paradosin hymon teresete). The verb 'set aside, nullify' (atheteo, G0114, queried 17 occurrences, consistently meaning to set aside, nullify, or reject) takes the commandment (entole) of God as its object, and the purpose clause introduced by 'in order that' (hina) makes tradition-keeping the motive. The ironic 'nicely' or 'well done' (Kalos) intensifies the indictment. The authority of the divine commandment is presupposed, not argued, and the rebuke is precisely that men nullify it for the sake of their tradition (paradosis).

The argument is grounded on a specific written text: 'For Moses said' (Mouses gar eipen) introduces the Decalogue command (Honor your father and mother) and the Exodus and Leviticus capital-sanction clause 'The one who speaks evil of father or mother let him surely die' (Ho kakologon patera e metera thanato teleutato). Jesus appeals to written-down Torah (instruction), not oral elaboration, to establish divine authority. The grammar forecloses an oral-tradition reading here: the citation formula points to what stands written.

Climactic indictment: 'rendering void the word of God by your tradition which you have handed down' (akyrountes ton logon tou theou te paradosei hymon he paredokate). 'Render legally void' (akyroo, G0208) is a forensic verb meaning to render legally void, and it occurs only 4 times across just 3 verses (Matthew 15:6, Mark 7:13, Galatians 3:17), in every case of voiding a prior authoritative text. The cognate verb 'you handed down' (paredokate, from paradidomi) sits beside the noun 'tradition' (paradosis), exposing the human chain of transmission as the agent of nullification. 'And many such similar things you do' (kai paromoia toiauta polla poieite) generalizes the pattern. The word-level claim is direct: tradition cannot annul the word (logos) of God (theos), and where the two clash the tradition is the violation.

The Bereans 'received the word' (edexanto ton logon, the apostolic preaching of Paul) 'with all eagerness' (meta pases prothymias), 'judicially examining the writings' (anakrinontes tas graphas) 'whether these things were so' (ei echoi tauta houtos). 'Judicially examine' (anakrino, G0350) is a courtroom term, and its queried distribution clusters in Luke, Acts, and 1 Corinthians in forensic or court-examination contexts, so the sense here is examine and adjudicate, not merely read. The input under examination is living apostolic speech; the standard is the prior writings (graphai). The narrative explicitly commends this stance as 'more noble' (eugenesteroi). At the word level, prior written revelation is the norm even for apostolic preaching.

'Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable toward teaching, toward refutation, toward correction, toward training in righteousness' (pasa graphe theopneustos kai ophelimos pros didaskalian, pros elegmon, pros epanorthosin, pros paideian ten en dikaiosyne). 'God-breathed' (theopneustos, G2315) is a verbal adjective and a true hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, queried 1 occurrence in the whole canon), rooting the writings' authority in divine origin rather than human reception. 'Writing, Scripture' (graphe, G1124) is the stable technical term for the writings and is spread across the whole New Testament (queried across 13 books), so its referent is not in doubt. The fourfold 'toward' (pros) series enumerates the functional offices that make Scripture the operative norm for teaching (didaskalia), refutation, restoration, and ethical formation, and 'every Scripture' (pasa graphe) is universal in scope. One genuine grammatical ambiguity exists: 'God-breathed' (theopneustos) may be read predicatively (every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable, that is, the linking verb 'is' is implied) or attributively (every God-breathed Scripture is also profitable). Both readings describe the same writings with the same functions and yield the same authority pattern.

'So that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped toward every good work' (hina artios e ho tou theou anthropos, pros pan ergon agathon exertismenos). The two completeness terms are both rare: 'complete' (artios, G0739) is a true hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, queried 1 occurrence) and the perfect participle, that is, a completed action whose result still stands, 'having been fully equipped' (exertismenos, from exartizo, G1822, queried only 2 occurrences, Acts 21:5 and here) means fully equipped. The purpose clause introduced by 'in order that' (hina) makes Scripture's sufficiency for the full equipping of the man (anthropos) of God the explicit goal of verse 16. 'Toward every good work' (pros pan ergon agathon) is exhaustive in scope. The honest caution is that the load-bearing completeness vocabulary is rare, so its precise nuance rests on these two clauses rather than on a broad concordance; the surrounding 'in order that' (hina) grammar and the 'every, all' (pas) quantifier, however, fix the direction firmly toward sufficiency.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'I urge you ... hold the traditions which you were taught either by our spoken word or by our letter' (parakalo ... krateite tas paradoseis has edidachthete eite dia logou eite di' epistoles hemon). The verb 'hold' (krateite) is the same one used negatively of human tradition in Mark 7:8, and the noun is the same dictionary form 'tradition' (paradosis, G3862). This is the strongest word-level complication, because it shows the very word condemned in Mark 7 being commanded here. The disambiguator is the 'of-X' grammatical form (the genitive) of origin: here the tradition is apostolic (handed down by the apostles' own spoken word or letter), the same content that becomes 'writing, Scripture' (graphe) within the canon. The dictionary form is morally neutral; its referent fixes its authority. The verse supports binding apostolic deposit but does not authorize a post-apostolic tradition stream operating parallel to or against the written word, which is the precise target of Mark 7:13's 'render legally void' (akyroo) indictment.

'I praise you ... that just as I delivered to you, you hold fast the traditions' (epaino de hymas ... kathos paredoka hymin tas paradoseis katechete). Same word-level phenomenon as 2 Thessalonians 2:15: 'tradition' (paradosis) from an apostle, delivered by direct first-generation transmission. The verb 'I delivered' (paradidomi) in Paul's mouth identifies the content as apostolic deposit. Queried distribution confirms the dual pattern of the one dictionary form: commended in 1 Corinthians 11:2, 2 Thessalonians 2:15, and 2 Thessalonians 3:6, condemned in Mark 7, Matthew 15, Colossians 2:8, and Galatians 1:14. God-originated and apostle-delivered is binding; human-originated and contrary to the commandment is nullifying.

'No prophecy of Scripture comes from one's own interpretation' (pasa propheteia graphes idias epilyseos ou ginetai). Sometimes invoked against private examination of Scripture, but the 'of-X' grammatical form 'of one's own interpretation' (idias epilyseos) together with the verse 21 explanation (men spoke 'being borne by the Holy Spirit', hypo pneumatos hagiou pheromenoi) places the origin of prophecy, not the venue of its reading, at issue. This does not undercut Acts 17:11's commendation of 'judicially examining' (anakrino) the writings (graphai). Together the two affirm that Scripture's origin is divine, so it judges other claims, while the reader's task is to test speech against Scripture.

Many other things Jesus did that are not written. At the word level this is a comment on the selectivity of the written record, not on extra-canonical authority. The verse names no parallel oral channel claiming jurisdictional parity with the written 'Scripture' (graphe); it concedes a scope-limit while verses 20 to 24 vouch for the truthfulness of what is written.

the church is 'pillar and support of the truth' (stylos kai hedraioma tes aletheias). The 'of-X' grammatical form 'of the truth' (tes aletheias) makes the church's function supportive, not generative: the truth is the prior reality the church upholds. The same Pauline corpus to Timothy contains the God-breathed nature (theopneustia) of Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16) and the same pastoral examination pattern (Acts 17:11's 'judicially examine', anakrino). The pillar holds up the truth; the truth, anchored at the word level to 'God-breathed Scripture' (graphe theopneustos), is what judges.

'See that no one takes you captive through philosophy ... according to the tradition of men' (blepete me tis hymas estai ho sylagogon dia tes philosophias ... kata ten paradosin ton anthropon). This is added in this pass as a third negative occurrence of 'tradition' (paradosis, G3862) outside the Synoptic anchor, with the same 'of men' (ton anthropon) grammatical form as Mark 7:8. It confirms that the condemned sense of the dictionary form is not limited to Jesus' dispute with the scribes but recurs in the apostolic letters, strengthening rather than complicating the verdict. The complication it removes is the suspicion that the negative sense is a one-context idiom: it is a stable Pauline usage too.

variants.note: The bundle reports 'not in ECM scope' (that is, outside the critical edition of New Testament textual variants, the ECM apparatus) is true for the anchor books at these verses, and the only ingested ECM window (3 John) contains none of them, so no published CBGM (coherence-based genealogical method) data applies here. No variant unit in the standard apparatus for 2 Timothy 3:16 to 17, Acts 17:11, Mark 7:8 to 13, or BHS (Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia, the standard Hebrew text) Isaiah 8:20 disturbs the word-level pattern that grounds the verdict: 'tradition' (paradosis) against 'commandment' (entole) and 'word' (logos) of God (theos), 'every Scripture is God-breathed' (pasa graphe theopneustos), 'judicially examine' (anakrino) of writings (graphai), and the Hebrew 'instruction' (torah) and 'testimony' (teudah). The only notable reading question is the predicative versus attributive construal of 'God-breathed' (theopneustos) in 2 Timothy 3:16, which is a syntactic, not a manuscript, matter and does not change which writings are described or what functions they serve. The verdict therefore holds across all plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading each anchor in its own clause and then across the four texts, the recurring word-level move is that a prior written, God-originated deposit ('instruction' torah and 'testimony' teudah; 'Scripture' graphe; 'word' logos of God theos) is the fixed standard, and later voices (oracles, human tradition, even apostolic preaching) are judged by it using forensic verbs ('render legally void' akyroo; 'set aside, nullify' atheteo; 'judicially examine' anakrino). On this reading the proposition is affirmed: where Scripture and a later authority conflict on what Scripture addresses, Scripture holds.

This lens takes seriously that the same dictionary form 'tradition' (paradosis, G3862) is commanded in 1 Corinthians 11:2, 2 Thessalonians 2:15, and 2 Thessalonians 3:6, and that 2 Thessalonians 2:15 explicitly pairs spoken word with letter as equally to be held. Stated in its strongest form, the words themselves do not say that the only legitimate transmission of apostolic teaching is the written one; they affirm a deposit that came by both speech and writing. The word-level reply, not a tradition reply, is that the canon nowhere ranks a continuing non-apostolic oral stream alongside 'Scripture' (graphe), and the one word that could carry such a stream ('tradition', paradosis) is condemned wherever its origin is human (Mark 7, Colossians 2:8, Galatians 1:14). The vocabulary affirms an apostolic deposit but does not establish a self-standing post-apostolic tradition with parity to Scripture, so this lens qualifies the proposition's scope rather than denying its core.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict is reached by grammatico-historical reading (interpreting each text in its own grammar and historical setting) of each anchor in its immediate clause, then by 'analogy of Scripture' (analogia Scripturae, the practice of comparing Scripture with Scripture) across the four texts and their TSK (Treasury of Scripture Knowledge cross-reference set) and OpenBible cross-references. Progressive revelation is invoked only insofar as the New Testament authors treat the Hebrew 'writings' (graphai) as a fixed prior deposit (Acts 17:11; 2 Timothy 3:15 calls Timothy's childhood writings 'sacred letters' (hiera grammata)) and the apostolic deposit (1 Corinthians 11:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:15) is itself later named 'Scripture' (graphe) within the canon (2 Peter 3:16 ranks Pauline letters with 'the rest of the Scriptures' (tais loipais graphais)). No allegorical or fourfold reading is required; the word-level pattern is overt. The two competing lenses above are stated symmetrically: both rest on real queried distribution of 'tradition' (paradosis), and they differ on scope, not on whether written Scripture norms what contradicts it.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Where Scripture and any other authority (tradition, church council, ecclesial office, or personal experience) conflict on a matter Scripture addresses, which holds the final word?
stem_audit.notes: The stem's phrasing 'final and supreme authority above all tradition, councils, and personal experience' echoes a confessional formulary, and the explicit triad ('tradition, councils, and personal experience') is itself a later polemical inventory rather than a biblical idiom. Two clarifications keep the treatment honest. First, the word-level pattern in the anchors concerns Scripture against human tradition that contradicts the divine commandment (Mark 7:8 to 13) and Scripture as the examination standard for apostolic preaching (Acts 17:11); the words do not address the modern category of 'church council' directly, since the New Testament's one quasi-conciliar moment (Acts 15) itself reasons by appeal to prophetic Scripture (Acts 15:15 to 18). Second, the canon does affirm apostolic 'tradition' (paradosis) (1 Corinthians 11:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:15), so the verdict concerns the relation of Scripture to non-apostolic post-canonical tradition, not the existence of authoritative apostolic transmission. Tagging the stem as VERDICT-CHANGED: verdict-preloaded does not change the word-level verdict, which is derived on the original stem; it flags that the stem's exhaustive triad imports a later taxonomy into a text-level question. Verdict 'affirms' is unchanged from the prior evidence file; the deepened queries ('tradition' (paradosis) dual pattern; 'render legally void' (akyroo) only at Matthew 15:6, Mark 7:13, and Galatians 3:17; 'God-breathed' (theopneustos) and 'complete' (artios) each a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible (a hapax); 'testimony' (teudah) near-hapax with a divergent Ruth 4:7 sense) confirm rather than alter it.

lay_summary: Four passages anchor the question and they all point the same way. In Isaiah 8:20 the Hebrew pairs 'instruction' (torah, written instruction) with 'testimony' (teudah) and tells the reader to test every speaker against this prior word; anyone who does not speak according to it has 'no dawn' (ein shachar) coming. In Mark 7:8 to 13 Jesus draws a clean line using two 'of-X' grammatical forms (genitives): the 'commandment' (entole) of God on one side, the 'tradition' (paradosis) of men (anthropoi) on the other. The verbs are blunt. They forsake, 'set aside' (atheteo), and 'render legally void' (akyroo) the commandment so they can keep the tradition. The word translated 'render legally void' (akyroo) is a courtroom term meaning to render void, and in the whole New Testament it appears only three places, always of voiding a prior authoritative text. The point is not that all tradition is bad but that when human transmission collides with what God (theos) has spoken in writing, the writing wins. In Acts 17:11 the Bereans are called more noble because they received Paul's preaching and then 'judicially examined' (anakrino) the writings (graphai), using a courtroom word for examination, to see whether his preaching matched. Even apostolic preaching gets tested against prior written Scripture. In 2 Timothy 3:16 to 17 the foundation is stated outright: every 'Scripture' (graphe) is 'God-breathed' (theopneustos, a word used nowhere else in the canon, that is, a hapax) and useful for teaching (didaskalia), rebuke, correction, and training, so that the man of God is 'complete' (artios) and fully equipped for every good work. Now the honest part, which is also why readers diverge. The one word the Bible uses for tradition (paradosis) is the same in the verses that condemn it and the verses that command it; Paul tells the Thessalonians to hold the traditions he handed down by word or letter. The word itself does not settle the matter. What settles it in the text is the origin the grammar attaches: God-given and apostle-delivered tradition is binding, while tradition labeled 'of men' (ton anthropon) is what gets nullified. So the divergence is not about whether Scripture judges what contradicts it; it is about how far an apostolic deposit extends and whether any later, non-apostolic stream stands beside the written word. On the words alone, the canon affirms the deposit but never ranks a separate ongoing tradition equal to Scripture.
